claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed, thin, amorphous iron oxide passive layer.
The integrity of Q235 steel's native iron oxide passive layer governs its corrosion resistance at both room temperature and 700–900 °C.
At room temperature, the amorphous passive film limits corrosion by acting as a barrier to corrosive species.
High-temperature salt exposure thermally destabilizes the native amorphous iron oxide layer.
At high temperature, the native oxide layer dissolves or transforms into less-protective crystalline phases.
Failure of the oxide layer increases exposure of the underlying Q235 steel to salt-induced corrosion and accelerates degradation.
Controlled annealing can transform Q235 steel's native amorphous oxide into a thicker, more crystalline oxide film.
The annealing-induced crystalline oxide film is more thermodynamically stable than the native amorphous film.
The annealing-induced oxide resists phase transformation and dissolution during high-temperature salt exposure.
Untreated Q235 steel will show greater mass loss and more severe corrosion after high-temperature salt exposure than after room-temperature exposure.
Annealed Q235 steel will show less high-temperature mass loss and corrosion damage than untreated Q235 steel.
The proposed mechanism applies when the native oxide film is the primary corrosion barrier.
Alloying elements or protective coatings can cause corrosion behavior to be governed by mechanisms other than native iron-oxide stability.
Additional alloying elements or protective coatings that dominate corrosion behavior are absent from the proposed Q235 specimens.
Untreated Q235 steel has established room- and high-temperature corrosion rates and oxide characteristics suitable for use as a baseline.

contradictions.description: The intervention treats increased oxide crystallinity as intrinsically stabilizing and protective, whereas the mechanism states that high-temperature transformation of the amorphous oxide into crystalline forms makes it less protective. No oxide phase, chemistry, or morphology is specified to reconcile why one crystallization route is protective and the other is not.
